transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I… I guess I’m here because I’ve been having some thoughts that scare me. Like, sometimes I think it would be easier if I just didn’t wake up. And on the drive home I catch myself wondering if my family, or my students, might be better off without me.

I don’t want to do anything. But the fact I’m thinking it at all… it frightened me.
Have you been feeling down or depressed?
Yeah… I think so. It’s hard to explain. I’ve just felt really low lately.
Before this recent period, have you felt this same kind of low mood for most of the last two years?
Not… most of the last two years, no. It’s been about a year and a half, maybe a bit more. Since I took on the STEM assessment redesign on top of my usual teaching load.
Do you feel these low feelings started because of the added STEM assessment redesign work?
I think so, yes. It seemed to start around then… when I took over the STEM assessment redesign on top of my normal teaching. That was about a year and seven months ago.
If that STEM redesign work were taken away, do you think you would still feel this low?
I don’t really know. I mean… I’d like to think I’d feel better, but I’m not sure it would just go away.
When you’re away from the STEM redesign work, do your mood symptoms ease up?
I’m not sure. I don’t think I’ve really paid close attention to whether it lifts when I’m away from it. Maybe a little sometimes, but… I can’t say clearly.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah… I think so. I used to look forward to things like softball, book club, my garden, even robotics club. Lately I mostly just… show up and go through the motions, or I cancel. It doesn’t really feel enjoyable anymore.
Do these low feelings ever happen on days when the STEM redesign work is completely off your mind?
I’m not sure. I think… sometimes my mind isn’t really on it, and I still feel low, but I haven’t kept track of that very clearly.
For at least two weeks, have you been feeling down like this nearly every day?
Yes… it’s been pretty much like this for a long time. Not just two weeks. Since I took on the STEM assessment redesign with my normal teaching load… about a year and a half, maybe a little more.
During the past month, have you had days when you felt this low even when nothing stressful was happening that day?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t been paying close enough attention to whether the day itself was stressful or not. I just know I’ve felt low a lot.
Have you been worrying excessively about a number of different things?
I don’t know… I mean, I worry, but I’m not sure I’d say it’s about a number of different things. I haven’t really thought about it that way.
When you think about what’s making you feel this low, does it seem mainly connected to the STEM assessment redesign work?
I’m not sure. It’s… it’s the easiest thing to point to, I guess, but I don’t know if it’s the whole reason.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Yes… I have. I’ll be exhausted, but then I just lie there thinking about assessment deadlines or things I got wrong in class. And I’ve been waking up around 4 a.m. and not really getting back to sleep.
Have you noticed a change in your appetite?

Yeah… I think so. On school days I often just don’t eat until really late, like the afternoon. I don’t really mean to. And my clothes have been looser… over the year, I suppose. I’m not trying to lose weight.
Have you been having trouble concentrating?

Yes… it’s been harder. I’ll read the same student response three or four times and still not really know what score to give it. Even small decisions, like which lab supplies to order, can sort of stop me for ages.
Have you been feeling unusually tired or low on energy?
Yes. By the time I’ve got through teaching and a department meeting, I feel… really heavy. Like even making dinner or answering a few parent emails feels like climbing a hill.
Have you been feeling worthless, or blaming yourself a lot?

Yeah… I do. I tend to blame myself a lot. If a lesson doesn’t go well, or a student looks confused, I sort of take it as… proof that I’m letting everyone down. Then I keep going over it in my head, like I’m a terrible teacher. And… a terrible mother, too.
During this past year and a half, has there been a stretch of at least two months when you felt mostly back to your usual self?
No… not really. It’s been pretty continuous. I’d say about a year and seven months now, since I took on the STEM assessment redesign on top of my normal teaching load.
Have these symptoms made it hard for you to function in your daily life?

Yes… it has. I’m falling behind on grading and planning, more than I want to admit. It’s starting to affect my classes.

There was a grading mistake recently that really shook me, because I used to be… very careful with that kind of thing. And outside of school, I’ve kind of stopped showing up for people. Friends, family. Mostly I just get through the day and go home exhausted.
Before this started a year and a half ago, was there ever another time in your life when you felt depressed like this for at least two weeks?
I… I’m not sure. I don’t really remember another time that was like this, at least not clearly. Maybe I had rough periods, but… I don’t know if it was for two weeks or anything like that.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient meets criteria for a depressive episode with depressed mood, anhedonia, insomnia, appetite/weight loss, poor concentration/indecisiveness, fatigue, excessive guilt/worthlessness, and passive death thoughts, persisting nearly daily for well over two weeks with clear functional impairment. Recurrent depressive disorder is not established because prior episodes are not confirmed. Persistent mood disorder/dysthymia is less likely because the syndrome includes a full major depressive episode picture rather than chronic lower-grade depression, though the long duration raises consideration. Adjustment disorder was considered because symptoms began after taking on a major work stressor, but symptoms are sustained, severe, and not clearly limited to or resolving with the stressor, favoring depressive episode.
